title: Where does the edge disappear?

beats.say: An inspection camera sees a seam between two finishes on a metal panel. The yellow window cuts out nine pixels. On the right you can see exactly what lies inside it.
Move the window one pixel right. Move it right again. At each stop, count the bright pixels in the right column and subtract the count in the left column. Which stop gives zero?

Window C. Its left and right columns are both bright. Three minus three gives zero. Follow this window through the camera, and you'll be able to tell which pixel changes a score and where an error signal goes back.

title: Brightness and arrangement tell different stories

beats.say: Each sensor square records brightness. Zero is dark and one is bright. Its row and column locate that reading on the panel. Cut out three rows and three columns and you keep the neighbors together.
Compare these two patches. Both contain the same total brightness. One is uniform, while the other has a boundary. Our detector needs a comparison across space to tell those arrangements apart.

title: Build a comparison between the two sides

beats.say: A filter, or kernel, is a small table of weights. Subtract the left column. Ignore the center column. Add the right column. These hand-chosen weights measure whether the patch becomes brighter toward the right.
Try the uniform patch first. Each pixel is two thirds as bright as white. The left side contributes minus two, and the right contributes plus two. What survives when those contributions meet? Zero.

Now use the edge patch with the same total brightness. Its dark left side contributes zero. Its bright right side contributes three. The response is three. We chose these weights to find this edge. During training, backpropagation tells the network how to adjust its filter weights.

title: Follow one response into its map cell

beats.say: Park the window in the top left. Multiply each pixel by the weight at the same address. Read the nine products one row at a time. How many units will enter the first output cell?
The total is three. Print it in the top-left cell of the feature map. An address on this map tells you where the window started. Keep the stencil and slide the window to measure the next patch.
Look at the third window, filled entirely with bright pixels. Its sides cancel. Where does that zero belong on the map?

title: Reuse the same weights at every position

beats.say: The zero goes in the top-right cell. Finish the scan row by row. A new patch comes under the same stencil, and each response lands at the matching address on the map.

Only three starting rows and three starting columns fit. They produce a three-by-three feature map. Local connectivity limits each measurement to its patch; weight sharing lets one learned rule serve every valid location.

title: Which window fits the bright mark?

beats.say: Here the camera sees a bright mark on a gray panel. Our first detector compared left and right. This one compares rows. Its middle row rewards brightness. Its top and bottom rows subtract it. We chose those weights by hand and set the bias to zero. How many places can the whole stencil fit?

Two starts across and two down. At the upper left the top row contributes minus point one one four. The bright middle row adds two point one one two. The bottom row subtracts one point one four six. Together they give point eight five two.

Try changing one weight while the window stays put. Set the upper-left weight to zero. Its pixel used to subtract three hundredths. Removing that penalty raises the response by three hundredths. At a fixed window you can correct the old sum by multiplying the aligned pixel by the change in its weight.

Put the original weight back. Slide the same stencil right, down and across to finish the map. The strongest match is at the bottom right. PyTorch slides the stored weights in this orientation. That's cross-correlation. Mathematical convolution flips the stencil across both axes first.
Our ridge stencil looks the same after a flip. An asymmetric imported filter can change its answer. A freely learned filter can learn either orientation.

title: Who owns the filter weights?

beats.say: Consider a color panel photo, two hundred twenty-four pixels on a side. A dense layer with two hundred fifty-six outputs gives every output a weight for every color value, plus a bias. That's over thirty-eight million parameters.
Give a local detector nine pixels in each of the three colors and one bias. Sixteen such filters need four hundred forty-eight parameters.

Those layers produce different things. One gives global scores. The other gives sixteen maps. Hold the map shapes fixed at two hundred twenty-two by two hundred twenty-two. Give every position its own private bank. How many times must we store the same size bank?
Forty-nine thousand two hundred eighty-four banks. That costs over twenty-two million parameters. Tie all those positions back to one shared bank, and the count returns to four hundred forty-eight.

Follow one local window. Move it one pixel right. Its neighbors change, but it uses the same weights. The window sets which pixels an output reads. Sharing sets how many copies of the weights you have to learn. Flattening the photo preserves its pixels and their order.
A dense layer would have to learn the reuse from examples. To compare speed, time the layers on the hardware you plan to use.

title: Does the peak follow the edge?

beats.say: Move the boundary one pixel right. Find the two columns that lit up in the old map. Both move one place in the new map. We call that translation equivariance. At stride one, away from the image border, the response follows the pattern.

Scan the map in reading order. Keep the largest value seen so far. After the ninth cell, that's the global maximum. Both crops have a peak of three. That one number tells you the detector fired somewhere. Its address is gone.

Move the boundary beyond the right edge of the crop. All five columns now show the dark finish. The windows that used to cross the seam have lost it. At a finite image border, even the global maximum can change.

Try a detector just two pixels wide on a single row. Subtract the left pixel from the right. Step two pixels at a time. The brackets show every pair it gets to read. The first pair straddles the edge. Now move the edge one place right, keeping the brackets fixed. Will the strongest response survive?

Read the same three pairs again. First read zero against zero. In the next pair, compare one with one. The last pair is also one against one. Every difference is zero, so the peak disappears. The edge is still there, between the brackets. At stride two, a one-pixel shift can change what the detector even gets to measure.

title: Where can the whole window fit?

beats.say: Back on the five-by-five image, use the original three-by-three filter. Move two cells at a time, both across and down. Four complete windows fit. That's where the two rows and two columns of this map come from.

Return to steps of one pixel. The unpadded image gives us three starts on each axis. Now add a ring of zeros. Look at the window over the top edge. Two bright pixels meet positive weights. What will this cell of the map read?
The top row sits in the padding, so all three products there are zero. Below it, each bright pixel in the right column adds one. Every other product is zero. The sum is plus two.
Move the window to the bottom right. The filter still subtracts on the left and adds on the right. Which side now touches the bright pixels that count? Predict the sign.
The right column and the bottom row lie in the padding. The two pixels on the left that touch the image each contribute minus one. The sum is minus two.
Fill in the other responses. The padded image is seven cells wide. Count the starts where a three-wide window fits. Five across and five down, including starts that touch the border.
With adjacent weights, subtract the kernel width from the padded width, divide by the stride, round down and add one for the first start.

title: Count starts using the complete kernel footprint

beats.say: Stride changes the gap between starts. Dilation changes the gap between weights inside one placement. A three-by-three kernel at dilation two still has nine weights, but spans five-by-five positions. Its effective span is dilation multiplied by the quantity kernel size minus one, then plus one.
Slide that five-pixel footprint along a row of twenty-eight pixels. Before you count, put its rightmost weight on the last pixel. Where is the first weight?
On pixel twenty-three, counting from zero. Starts zero through twenty-three give twenty-four placements.
For each axis, take the padded length, subtract the effective span and divide by the stride. Round down and add one to count the first placement.

At stride one, same-size padding adds a total of dilation multiplied by the quantity kernel size minus one extra positions, split across the two sides. An odd total requires unequal sides. PyTorch same padding supports stride one. For valid padding there are no synthetic positions.
Shape checks require positive kernel, stride and dilation, nonnegative padding, and a footprint that fits the padded input.

title: Several input channels contribute to one output

beats.say: A color image has several input channels. Our small example uses two. One output filter has a kernel for each channel. Compute each patch sum, then add the contributions. Here, three plus three gives one output value of six. We use zero bias.

A second output filter gets its own weights. Reverse the first channel kernel and retain the second. The channel contributions become minus three and plus three, so this filter gives zero at the same position. Multiple filters create multiple output maps.

title: One output sums only its declared input-channel group

beats.say: With groups one, each output filter sees all input channels. Its stored shape is output channels by input channels by kernel height by kernel width. Add one bias per output filter.
A batch keeps its own axis: batch, input channels, height, width becomes batch, output channels, output height, output width. Each image in the batch gets its own six output maps.

Split the channels into two groups. Each filter sees input channels divided by groups, and both channel counts must divide evenly by the group count. With four inputs, six outputs, two groups and three-by-three weights, each output reads two channels.
Six times two times nine, plus six biases, gives one hundred fourteen parameters. A change in the first input can now reach only the three filters in its group.

In general the parameter count is output channels multiplied by input channels divided by groups, multiplied by kernel height and width, then plus output biases when enabled. Double the image width and the same weights slide farther. Change stride or dilation and those weights sample different pixels. The layer still stores one hundred fourteen parameters.

title: How many original pixels can one output see?

beats.say: Look along one row of the panel. The yellow bracket covers three pixels. Slide the window one pixel to the right. Its center moves one pixel too. The input pixels a window can use form its receptive field.

The distance between neighboring centers, in input pixels, is the jump. A second three-by-three filter reads three neighboring windows along this row. How many different pixels do they cover together?

Five pixels. Start with three. Each slide adds one. Now pool two neighboring outputs. Each covers five of the original pixels. Together they cover six. At stride two, watch the next pooled window slide over. Its center moves two input pixels.

The next three-by-three filter reads three pooled outputs. Each covers six pixels and their starts are two pixels apart. Follow the three brackets. How far is it from the first bracket's left edge to the last bracket's right edge?
Start with the first six pixels. The middle bracket adds another two. The last two extend the right edge once more. Six plus two plus two gives ten.
A three-wide filter spans two gaps. For each gap, add dilation times the old jump to the field. Multiply the old jump by stride to get the new jump. A wider field can combine distant marks.
A zero weight or an inactive unit blocks a path inside that field. At the image border, the window can also reach into padding. Now look at the pooling row. It keeps all thirty-two channels.
The map shrinks from two hundred twenty positions across to one hundred ten. That leaves fewer places to locate a narrow scratch.

title: What should the pool remember?

beats.say: Here are sixteen responses from another image. Take the strongest response in each square of four. Start in the upper left. Which number would you keep?

Keep point nine one. Move right for the next peak. Then take the lower left and the lower right. Each window sends one number on. That's max pooling. The windows step two cells at a time and use no trainable weights.

Save the row and column beside each peak. Count from zero. The upper-right output came from row one, column two. That address will matter on the way back. With average pooling, add the four responses and divide by four. See how the isolated peak gets diluted in the mean.
Go back to max pooling. Suppose the very first cell now ties the peak in its window. The pooled value stays the same. Can the value alone tell you which address to save?

Both cells qualify. Our NumPy example takes the first maximum in flattened order, reading across each row. The tile saves row zero, column zero. Return to the untied map. Swap the peak with its left neighbor. The value stays in the same pooled cell. Swap it across the boundary instead. The upper-right window now gets the peak.

title: Where does the minus sign go?

beats.say: Back on the original map, each window had a single winner. The values on the right now tell us how sensitive the loss is to each pooled output. Find minus one. Its tile still has the saved address. Which input should receive that minus sign?

Follow it back to the cell that supplied the peak. The sign comes along. Two goes back to the upper-left window's winner. The other two gradients return to their own winners. Every other entry stays zero.
These numbers tell an earlier layer how changing a response would affect the loss. Backward leaves the responses themselves in place.

Now use an average in each of the same windows. Take minus one again. The mean gives each input a weight of one quarter. Split the gradient into four equal shares and send one to each input. They all keep the minus sign.
Apply the same division to the other three windows. With padding, use the number of cells the pooling rule actually averages.

Bring the windows one cell closer together. On this three-by-three grid the center belongs to all four windows. Each window still sends a quarter of its gradient to each member. Follow the four shares into the center. Even the negative share counts.
Their sum is one and one eighth. When paths meet, each path contributes to the same input gradient.

title: What did the backward pass lose?

beats.say: Keep those overlapping windows. Switch from taking the mean to keeping the largest response. Here the center is nine. Slide over the four possible starts. Each window picks the same cell. Reading the input across each row from zero, its flat index is four. PyTorch saves that index for all four outputs.

Run a faulty backward pass. It assigns each incoming gradient to the saved cell. Watch which value survives after two, minus one, a half, and three have arrived. The center holds three. Which contributions did that assignment erase?

Each assignment replaced the previous value. Start again from zero. Add each incoming gradient to what's already there. Watch the negative one bring two down to one. The half brings it to one and a half. Now add the last three. The center receives four and a half. Every other input receives zero.

This is what plus-equals buys you in a backward loop. All four signed paths reach the earlier layer. The article checks both pieces on the CPU with PyTorch, the four saved indices and the accumulated center gradient. Max pooling itself still has no weights to update.

title: Collapse spatial positions while preserving channels

beats.say: Global average pooling gives each channel its own mean. Average height and width within each example. The output has a batch axis and a channel axis. Some implementations keep two spatial axes of length one. Rearrange the nine numbers within a channel. The mean stays put, so the head loses that location information. A shift at the edge of a finite image can change the numbers before pooling.
A Q-class head after flattening uses channels times height times width times Q weights, plus Q biases. After global average pooling it uses channels times Q weights, plus the same Q biases.

For a supplied six-channel three-by-three map and two classes, those counts are one hundred ten and fourteen. Both heads still produce two logits per example, but their allowable use of spatial position differs.

Look at the single bright response on the left. A nine sits among eight zeros. Max pooling keeps the nine. Average pooling divides the sum by nine and returns one. When a mark covers just one cell, the choice of pooling changes what reaches the classifier.

title: A boundary pixel belongs to fewer valid windows

beats.say: Place a single unit signal in a five-by-five image and use an all-ones three-by-three kernel. With valid stride-one placements, the corner signal belongs to one window. Move that same signal to the center, and it belongs to nine.
Light one map cell for each window that contains the mark. Each of those responses is one. Add the map and you count how many times the mark contributed.

Keep the signal at the corner and add one zero border. Four complete windows can now contain it, so the aggregate becomes four. On the article’s smaller four-by-four crop, even central pixels belong to at most four valid windows. Only two starts fit across that smaller crop and two fit down.

Padding lets four windows see the corner mark. Look at what else those windows see. Some of their pixels come from the border we added. An edge detector compares those added pixels with the real ones.

title: Where did the edge on a gray panel come from?

beats.say: Every pixel on this panel is the same gray, point six. The filter adds the top row and subtracts the bottom row. In the middle of the panel the two rows cancel. Slide up to the black padding. The top row now adds zero.
The bottom row still subtracts one point eight. The filter has found the edge of the padding.

Keep the camera image and change the padding to reflection. The border borrows its gray from one row inside the panel. Each top pixel now matches the one below the center. Every window cancels. The largest absolute response is zero.

Put a bright stripe one row inside the panel. Compare the same top window under both rules. Zero padding leaves black above the stripe. Reflection copies the stripe into the border. Its two bright rows cancel.
When you trace a score near the edge, check which pixels came from the camera and which came from padding. Use the same padding in training and on the camera.

title: Which response sets both class scores?

beats.say: Return to the gray panel with the bright center. Here are its four ridge responses. First apply ReLU, which replaces any negative value with zero. All four pass through. Only one number can leave the pool. Which window will set both class scores?

The bottom right has the largest response. Save its address and send its value to both outputs. The first head weight is positive. Multiply by one point four, then subtract two tenths. The second weight is negative. Multiply by minus nine tenths, then add one tenth.
A change in this one pooled feature pushes the two scores in opposite directions.

These raw scores are logits. In the article, NumPy and PyTorch use the same hand-picked weights. Their CPU results agree within one millionth. That checks the arithmetic. To find out whether these scores identify cracks, we'd need labeled photos the model hasn't seen.

Follow the tensor shapes. The article calls unsqueeze twice to add a batch axis for the one photo and a channel axis for grayscale. The convolution leaves two rows and two columns. Pooling leaves one spatial value. Flatten that to one feature and the head returns two logits.

ReLU matters on other crops. Take two possible signed responses, minus point four and plus point four. ReLU clips the first to zero and keeps the second. Stack affine convolutions alone and their composition stays affine, even when strides or boundaries prevent writing it as one ordinary shared convolution.

title: Add a learned change to an identity with matching shape

beats.say: Some deeper plain networks in the ResNet experiments had higher training error than their shallower counterparts. The authors called this degradation. They reported healthy gradient norms in the batch-normalized plain networks. An identity shortcut gives the input a direct route to an addition.
Suppose one saved input value is two and the branch learns a change of minus one. Bring them together. The sum is one. The branch only has to supply the change.

Follow the article’s basic block: three-by-three convolution, batch normalization, ReLU, another convolution and normalization, then add the saved identity and apply ReLU. Padding one preserves its spatial size. Sixteen channels in and out keep the addition compatible.

If the branch changes from sixteen channels to thirty-two, can the saved input still be added directly? Give the shortcut a one-by-one projection with thirty-two outputs. If the branch also downsamples, the shortcut needs the same spatial output size.

Batch normalization computes per-channel statistics across batch and spatial positions, then applies learned scale and offset. With its default settings, training updates running estimates that evaluation reuses. The article’s new block runs in training mode and preserves shape one by sixteen by twenty-eight by twenty-eight.
That gives the addition one matching value on each path at every position.

title: The direct gradient path can still cancel or be gated

beats.say: For the sum y equals F of x plus x, the branch Jacobian and identity add. Multiply the incoming gradient by that combined map. In a supplied scalar slice, branch slope zero point two plus identity one gives one point two.
An incoming gradient three becomes three point six. This derivative concerns the sum before the final activation.

Change the branch slope to minus one. Its minus three cancels the identity's plus three. The total is zero. Both paths still carry a gradient. Now restore the original slope and make the sum negative. The post-addition ReLU is inactive. Its gate stops the incoming gradient before it reaches either path.

Residual learning supported the original paper’s fifty-, one-hundred-one- and one-hundred-fifty-two-layer experiments. LeNet demonstrated learned convolutional features for document recognition, and AlexNet for large-scale image classification.

title: The same patch projection can be written as a convolution

beats.say: A vision transformer begins by cutting nonoverlapping image patches and linearly projecting each flattened patch into a D-dimensional token. For a P-by-P RGB patch, the flat vector has three times P squared entries.
The same projection at every patch is a convolution with kernel P, stride P and D output channels, when coefficient ordering and bias agree.

Use a supplied four-by-four grayscale image, two-by-two patches and three output features. Each patch has four values, so the shared projection has twelve weights and three biases. Four patches produce four three-feature tokens.

Take the first row of projection weights. Fold it into two rows, keeping the flattened patch order. Its result is the first token feature. Do the same for the other two rows and add each feature's bias. A stride of two puts each answer at the next nonoverlapping patch.

Follow a patch after the projection. A convolution reads neighboring positions through a local window. In the original vision transformer, self-attention can mix any pair of patches. Even the two opposite corners can exchange information in one layer. A learned position vector tells the model where each patch came from.

title: What does the border reveal?

beats.say: The original ViT experiments benefited from large-scale pretraining. DeiT later obtained competitive ImageNet transformers without external training images using its training recipe and teacher distillation. ConvNeXt modernized convolutional design and competed with the transformers in its own experiments.

Test both candidates on the same held-out panel photos. Set aside photos with a tiny mark and photos with one at the border. A model can do well overall and still miss the defects that matter. Measure each slice and time inference on the target hardware. Keep the resize, padding and pooling settings with the measurements.

Take a toy inspection run with twelve labeled photos, each showing a defect. The model catches nine of ten center marks. It misses both border marks. Nine detections overall can hide zero out of two at the border. Before choosing this model, collect more border examples and compare that slice on both candidates.

title: Predict what reversing the edge will do

beats.say: Return to our opening windows. The two windows crossing the edge respond, and the uniformly bright one gives zero. Now predict the sign if we swap dark and bright everywhere. Keep the signed weights fixed.

Reverse the brightness. The left column now subtracts more than the right adds. The boundary responses become minus three. Library convolution layers usually apply this stored kernel orientation directly; our calculation follows that cross-correlation convention.
Apply ReLU. Replace each negative response with zero. With this filter, the dark-to-bright edge survives. Reverse the edge and its response drops to zero after ReLU.

title: Which window gets the gradient?

beats.say: Back at the panel camera, compare the two highest responses. The bottom right leads by twenty-two thousandths. Darken just the corner pixel, from point zero five to point zero one. Keep the ridge filter fixed. Which window can feel that change? Can it catch the leader?

Only the upper-left window covers that corner. The pixel fell by four hundredths. Multiply that change by the fixed weight, negative six tenths. A darker corner takes away some of the penalty. The upper-left response gains twenty-four thousandths. Add that gain to the original response. The new response is point eight seven six. Trace that step on the ruler.
The other three windows miss the corner, so their responses stay put. The upper left now leads by just two thousandths.

All four responses are positive, so ReLU passes them through. Use the new maximum in the two-class head. The first score edges up and the second edges down. Now send minus two back through max pooling. It goes to the upper left, the address saved on this pass.

Try a different exposure. Start again from the original crop. This time the corner goes from point zero five to point zero two. The same negative weight still applies. Where would you send minus two this time?

The corner lost three hundredths. Multiply the change by negative six tenths. The upper-left response gains eighteen thousandths. Add that gain to the original response. It stops at point eight seven zero. Trace that step on the ruler. The other three responses stay put. The bottom right still wins, so the pooled value and both class scores stay where they started.

Follow minus two back to the bottom right. Two nearly identical exposures sent the gradient to different windows. Trace the winner saved for this image before you send an error signal back. In the next lesson, backpropagation computes gradients. An optimizer uses those gradients to update the weights.
